# Yasoja Sutta (Ud 3.3 (PTS Ud 24))

**ID:** Ud 3.3 (PTS Ud 24)
**Section:** Udāna (ud)

**Title (Pali):** Yasoja Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Yasoja Sutta* (Ud 3.3) is the third discourse of the Nandavagga in the *Udāna* [Masefield 1997; Anandajoti Bhikkhu 2007]. Set at Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery in Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthī, the sutta opens when five hundred visiting monks headed by Venerable Yasoja arrive and create a loud commotion while greeting resident monks and arranging their dwellings and robes [Freedman 1977; Anandajoti Bhikkhu 2007; Sarada 2000]. Comparing their uproar to that of fishermen hauling in a catch of fish, the Buddha dismisses them from his presence [Freedman 1977; Anandajoti Bhikkhu 2007; Sarada 2000]. Acknowledging that the Master dismissed them out of compassion and concern for their welfare, Yasoja and the monks depart for the Vajjian country, construct leaf huts by the river Vaggumudā, and devote themselves to ardent practice during the rains retreat, all attaining the threefold knowledge (arahantship) [SuttaCentral; Freedman 1977; Masefield 1997; Horner 1971]. Following the retreat, the Buddha sends for the newly awakened monks [Anandajoti 2010; Horner 1971].

Scholars note that the narrative closely mirrors the *Cātuma Sutta* (MN 67), though the Udāna narrative features Yasoja rather than Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna, and emphasizes that the dismissal was an act of compassion that catalyzed the monks' awakening [SuttaCentral; Freedman 1977; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records verse parallels in the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* (UV 32, UVS 32, Uv Kg 32) and Chinese collections (T 212.33, T 213.32), as well as a reference in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.3.12) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal text reuse with the *Cātuma Sutta* (MN 67, sharing §1.3–5.1_1 with §2.1–5.2), as well as significant shared phrasing with AN 8, the *Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka* (Kd 19), the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), and the *Uposatha Sutta* (Ud 5.5) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of the text with Sanskrit Vinaya texts (*Śayanāsanavastu*, *Carmavastu*) and Chinese Āgama sūtras in T 26, T 64, T 99, and T 125 [DharmaNexus]. Commentarial traditions cross-reference Yasoja's background and verse connections across the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [Burlingame 1921; Horner 1971].
